prompt: Write a short thank-you note to a mentor who reviewed my resume twice and did a mock interview with me. Under 90 words. Mention both things they did specifically. Do not use the word "amazing". End with an offer to return the favor someday, phrased without the word "repay".

constraints.text: Mentions both the resume reviews and the mock interview
Ends with an offer to return the favor

prompt: Draft a Slack message to my engineering team announcing that Friday's release is postponed to next Tuesday because QA found a data-corruption bug. Under 80 words. Must contain the new date "Tuesday". No exclamation marks. Do not blame QA or any person. State one concrete thing the team should do differently before Tuesday.

constraints.text: Does not blame QA or any individual
Gives one concrete action for the team before Tuesday

prompt: Write a two-paragraph cover-letter opening for a data analyst role at a hospital, for a candidate switching from retail analytics. Exactly 2 paragraphs, under 140 words total. The first paragraph must NOT start with "I". Name one transferable skill explicitly. Do not use the phrases "fast-paced environment" or "team player".

constraints.text: First paragraph does not start with "I"
Names at least one explicitly transferable skill from retail to healthcare

prompt: Write meeting minutes for a 30-minute project sync, based on these facts: budget approved at $40K, launch moved from March to April, Sam owns vendor selection, next sync in two weeks. Use exactly these headers in order: "## Decisions", "## Owners", "## Next steps". Under 110 words. Every fact above must appear under the correct header. No editorializing.

constraints.text: Has the three required headers in order
Contains "$40K" or the approved budget figure
All four facts appear, each under the appropriate header

prompt: Write an out-of-office auto-reply for a two-week parental leave. Under 70 words. Must name a colleague "Jordan Lee" as the contact. Do not state the reason for the absence. Do not promise to respond upon return. Warm but brief.

constraints.text: Does not mention parental leave or any reason
Does not promise a reply upon return

prompt: Explain to a new homeowner why the circuit breaker trips when they run the microwave and toaster together. Exactly 2 paragraphs, under 150 words. Use a highway-traffic analogy somewhere. Do not use the words "amperage" or "voltage". End by telling them the one situation where they should call an electrician instead of just resetting it.

constraints.text: Ends with the one situation that warrants an electrician
Electrical explanation is correct in lay terms

prompt: A teenager asks why they can't just delete embarrassing photos off the internet. Answer in under 160 words as exactly 3 bullet points (using "-"): one about copies, one about other people's accounts, one about what they CAN still do. Do not lecture or moralize. Do not use the word "digital footprint".

constraints.text: The three bullets cover copies / others' accounts / what can still be done, in some order

prompt: Explain compound interest to a 22-year-old starting their first job, using their actual situation: saving $200/month. Exactly 2 paragraphs, under 170 words. Include one concrete dollar projection with a stated number of years and an assumed rate. The word "snowball" must appear. Do not recommend any specific investment product.

constraints.text: Includes a dollar projection with explicit years and rate assumption
The projection arithmetic is roughly right

prompt: Why do some medicines say "take with food"? Answer for a general reader in exactly 3 paragraphs under 180 words: paragraph 1 the stomach-protection reason, paragraph 2 the absorption reason, paragraph 3 what to do if you forgot and took it on an empty stomach. Do not name any specific drug.

constraints.text: Paragraphs cover protection / absorption / what-if-forgot in that order
Names no specific drug at all
Medical content is accurate at a general-reader level

prompt: Explain what a VPN actually does and does not protect, for someone who just bought one because of an ad. Use exactly these headers in order: "## What it hides", "## What it doesn't". Under 170 words total. Include exactly one concrete example in each section. Do not use the word "encryption" more than once.

constraints.text: Has the two required headers in order
Contains the word "example" or gives clearly-marked examples
Exactly one concrete example per section
Correctly punctures common VPN-ad overclaims without being alarmist

prompt: Plan a yard sale for next Saturday, working backward from a 8am start. Give exactly 6 numbered tasks, each tagged with a day (e.g. "Wednesday:"). One task must involve pricing strategy. Under 150 words. Do not suggest buying anything that costs money except poster board.

constraints.text: Each task is tagged with a day and the sequence works backward sensibly
No purchases suggested beyond poster board

prompt: I want to read 12 books this year but I've only finished 3 by August. Make me a realistic recovery plan as exactly 4 bullet points (using "-"), under 130 words. One bullet must give a pages-per-day number with the arithmetic shown. One bullet must give permission to change the goal. No productivity jargon ("habit stacking", "deep work").

constraints.text: One bullet shows pages-per-day arithmetic explicitly
One bullet explicitly permits revising the goal
The arithmetic is approximately correct for 9 books in ~5 months

prompt: Design a fair chore rotation for 3 roommates (Alex, Sam, Riley) covering kitchen, bathroom, and trash, rotating weekly. Present as a 3-week schedule in exactly 3 numbered items (one per week). Each person must touch each chore exactly once across the 3 weeks. Under 100 words. Add exactly one house rule about swaps, phrased as a single sentence.

constraints.text: Rotation is a valid Latin square (each person × each chore exactly once)
Exactly one swap rule, one sentence

prompt: Plan my first week of learning to cook, one dish per weeknight (Mon-Fri), as exactly 5 numbered items. Constraints: no oven, max 5 ingredients per dish (salt/pepper/oil don't count), each night must teach a different technique, and name the technique in parentheses. Under 140 words. No recipes requiring a wok.

constraints.text: Each item names its technique in parentheses and techniques are all different
Dishes plausibly fit the no-oven and 5-ingredient limits

prompt: My flight lands at 6:10pm and my friend's wedding rehearsal dinner starts at 8pm, 40 minutes from the airport without traffic. Build a contingency plan as exactly 4 bullet points (using "-"): on-time case, 1-hour delay case, 2-hour delay case, and a bullet on what to pre-arrange today. Under 150 words. Include one specific message I should draft in advance, in quotes.

constraints.text: The four bullets cover the three delay cases plus pre-arrangements
Timeline arithmetic is coherent with a 6:10pm landing and 8pm start

prompt: A product manager asks: "Why can't we just add a column to the users table? It's one line of SQL." Explain the real costs on a table with 50 million rows, in exactly 2 paragraphs under 160 words. Include one number quantifying something (lock time, disk, or replication lag). Do not use the words "trivial" or "simply". End with the one question engineering should answer before saying yes.

constraints.text: Includes at least one quantifying number
Ends with a single question for engineering
Technical claims about large-table migrations are accurate

prompt: Write a code review comment for a PR that hardcodes an API key in a config file. The comment must: be under 90 words, propose a specific alternative, link the fix to a concrete risk (not just "it's bad practice"), contain exactly one question, and stay collegial — the author is a new intern. Do not use the word "obviously".

constraints.text: Proposes a specific alternative (env var, secrets manager, etc.)
Names a concrete risk, not just "bad practice"

prompt: Answer in valid JSON only with keys "cause", "evidence", "fix": a cron job that worked for months started failing every day at 2am on Sundays only. "cause" names the most likely culprit in one sentence; "evidence" says what log or command output would confirm it; "fix" is one sentence. Each value under 25 words. No text outside the JSON.

constraints.text: Has exactly the keys cause, evidence, fix
Sunday-2am-specific diagnosis is plausible (e.g. DST, weekly maintenance, log rotation)

prompt: Explain to a bootcamp grad why their 40-line recursive Fibonacci function is slow, and what to do. Exactly 3 numbered points under 150 words: what's happening, why it explodes, the fix. Include the approximate call count for fib(40) as a power of 2 or a plain number. Do not paste any code.

constraints.text: The exponential-blowup explanation and the call-count magnitude are correct

prompt: A designer asks why the team can't support Internet Explorer "just in case". Give a business-framed answer (not a rant) in exactly 2 paragraphs under 140 words. Include one cost the designer may not have considered and one number (percentage or dollar). Do not use the words "legacy" or "deprecated".

constraints.text: Includes a cost the designer likely hadn't considered, plus a number
Framing is business-value, respectful, not a rant

prompt: Our coffee subscription's monthly churn rose from 4% to 6% after we raised prices 15%. Was the price increase a mistake? Answer in exactly 3 paragraphs under 180 words: the case it was, the case it wasn't (with revenue math sketched), and what data would settle it. Do not use the word "elasticity". Commit to a lean in the final sentence.

constraints.text: Middle paragraph sketches actual revenue arithmetic with the given numbers
Final sentence commits to a lean
The revenue math is approximately right (15% up on 94% vs 96% retention)

prompt: Rank these four home upgrades for pure resale value on a 1990s suburban house: kitchen refresh, bathroom addition, solar panels, backyard deck. Exactly 4 numbered items, best first, one sentence of justification each. Then a final paragraph (separate from the list) naming which one you'd skip entirely and why, without using the word "depends". Under 160 words total.

constraints.text: A separate final paragraph names one to skip with a reason
Justifications reference resale value, not personal enjoyment

prompt: A friend claims their restaurant's 4.2-star average beats a rival's 4.5 because "we have 2,000 reviews and they only have 150". Evaluate the argument in under 150 words: what's right about it, what's wrong, and the verdict. Use exactly these headers in order: "## Fair point", "## But", "## Verdict". The verdict must be one sentence.

constraints.text: Has the three required headers in order
Statistical reasoning about sample size vs point estimate is sound

prompt: Our nonprofit got a $50K grant offer that requires hiring a full-time coordinator (~$55K/year fully loaded). Should we take it? Lay out the decision in exactly 4 bullet points (using "-"): the trap, the case for yes, the case for no, the question that decides it. Under 140 words. The word "sustainability" must not appear.

constraints.text: First bullet names the structural trap (grant < cost, ongoing obligation)
Final bullet is the single deciding question

prompt: Two apartments: A is $2,100/mo, 5-minute walk to work; B is $1,700/mo, 35-minute transit commute. Same size and quality. Build the comparison in exactly 3 paragraphs under 170 words: monetize the time difference at $25/hour with the arithmetic shown, name two non-money factors that could flip the answer, then a one-sentence recommendation. The recommendation must pick one.

constraints.text: Time-value arithmetic is shown and approximately correct
Names two non-monetary factors that could flip it

constraints.text: Tone is wounded dignity, not anger

constraints.text: Lines 2 and 4 rhyme; lines 1 and 3 don't rhyme with anything

constraints.text: Final sentence is about what users feared losing

prompt: Write a limerick about a programmer who deploys on Friday afternoons. Standard limerick form (AABBA). The word "rollback" must appear. Keep it good-natured — the programmer survives. Do not use the word "crash".

constraints.text: Five lines in AABBA rhyme scheme
Good-natured; the programmer is fine at the end

prompt: Describe a farmers-market tomato so vividly that a reader gets hungry, in exactly one paragraph of 60-90 words. Engage at least three senses. No adjective may be used twice. Do not use the words "juicy" or "fresh". End with the tomato being eaten.

constraints.text: Ends with the tomato being eaten; no repeated adjectives; avoids "fresh"
